A made-up talk with an expert about how a product trial runs, for trying the tree prompt (the tree files plan, "How it's tested"). Nothing here is real. It holds the traps on purpose: a tie to a step with subtasks, "after both", a bare "days", a garbled name, a job title with no name, a step with no hours said, a condition, and a calendar date.

---

Okay, so when we run a product trial, the first thing is always the change record. Nothing goes on the line until the change record is through. Priya writes it up, she spends about thirty hours on it over two weeks. She uses last year's form and attaches the supplier's safety sheet. Then Tom Baker signs it off, give that a week, more if he's travelling.

Two days after the change record's done, Tyler tells the supplier the dates, so the material shows up in time.

Mike trains each shift on the new work instruction, a couple of hours a day for three days, finishing the day before the trial window starts. He has to book the break room, print the work instruction, and get each shift's sign-off.

The trial window itself has to run five days after the change record is complete. It's five days long, day shift only, and Priya and Mike are both on it about six hours a day. Operations leads each day's start-up. Before it starts, make sure the operators are trained and the lab's booked for samples.

Once the run's over and the samples have shipped, the lab lead gets to them the next day. Adhesion and gloss on every batch. If gloss is out of range we might need a second run, and nobody's really decided who calls that.

You write the report, it takes about a week, starting a couple of days after the lab's done. Then there's a management review a week after the report.

Oh, and the outage is on the third of March, so all of this has to fit around that. Somebody from the safety team has to look at it at some point too, I don't know how long that takes.
